title: Boralex went private in August and raised C$600M in public debt in November. Seven banks underwrote it.
paragraphs: The take-private closed on 14 August at C$37.25 a share, and the stock was delisted three days later. Boralex ceased to be a reporting issuer in every province. On the tracker's own framing, that was supposed to be the end of the public record.

It was not. On 13 November, Boralex agreed to issue C$600M of medium-term notes: C$250M of Series 1 at 4.503% to November 2031, and C$350M of Series 2 at 5.173% to November 2036. Morningstar DBRS rated them BBB with a stable trend. Proceeds repay the bridge facility that funded the buyout. The agency syndicate was BMO, CIBC, Desjardins, National Bank, RBC, Scotia and TD, with Brookfield Securities Canada alongside them.

That last detail is the one worth sitting with. The buyer's own dealer sat in the syndicate placing debt into the company it had just bought. The bridge-to-bond sequence is ordinary leveraged finance; what is less ordinary is seeing it laid out in a public release by a company that had just exited public reporting.

This cuts against the disclosure-cliff argument in the Method section, and the correction belongs here rather than buried in the changelog. Equity disclosure ended at delisting. Debt disclosure did not, because a private issuer selling rated notes into the Canadian private placement market still has to tell the market the coupon, the tenor and the rating. Innergex pruned its archive and went quiet. Boralex kept publishing, because it kept borrowing.

The practical read is that the private market record is more accessible through the credit side than the equity side. A Quebec issuer that goes private stops filing circulars but keeps issuing paper, and every issuance carries terms. For anyone trying to track these assets after they leave the exchange, the rating agencies and the note announcements are the surviving window.

title: The Innergex syndication shows the terms Quebec sets for outside money.
paragraphs: Most coverage of the Innergex take-private stopped at the headline. CDPQ paid C$13.75 a share, a 58% premium to the last close and 80% to the thirty-day average, for an enterprise value of C$10.0B. That number is the least interesting part of the transaction.

The structure is where the information sits. CDPQ said at announcement that it would seek to syndicate up to 20% of its invested capital, and that the deal was not conditional on doing so. It closed on 21 July 2025 having completed that syndication. Investissement Québec, Desjardins Global Asset Management and Fondaction came in. So did 14 Swiss institutional investors. CDPQ stayed the leading shareholder.

Read the sequence in order and the terms become explicit. The ceiling was set at 20% before any outside investor was approached. The domestic institutions were named first in the release. The foreign participants were admitted as a group, at the remaining size, into a company where the buyer had already secured control. And Hydro-Québec, holding roughly 19.9% going in, had signed a support and voting agreement before the process began. Roughly a fifth of the company was already committed to the outcome on day one.

Compare that to how the same money enters elsewhere. In a normal infrastructure syndication, a lead sponsor brings partners in to share risk and the allocation is a negotiation. Here the allocation was a policy. The Swiss investors did not compete for a larger position, because a larger position was never available.

Boralex confirms the pattern from the other direction. La Caisse lent to it, held equity in it, put C$250M of subordinated debt into it in July 2025, then took it private alongside Brookfield eight months later at 30% of the private company. Brookfield holds the majority and La Caisse holds a blocking-size minority, with the head office staying in Quebec. Even the largest alternative asset manager in the world entered on those terms.

The practical read for a lender or a sponsor is not that Quebec is closed. Foreign capital is clearly welcome, and it is getting deployed. It is that the size and the shape of the position are usually decided before the conversation starts. Ask early who already holds a stake and what they have signed, because in this market that often determines what is left rather than what is negotiable.

This reads five transactions. The test is A/O 2026-01, where bids close in February. If the winning consortia are domestic-led with foreign capital in minority positions behind them, the pattern holds. If a foreign sponsor wins outright, it does not.

title: Hydro-Québec is funding the 2035 plan with 40-year bonds, and every Canadian dealer is in the syndicate.
paragraphs: On 7 August, Hydro-Québec reopened its Series JU bonds for another C$500M. The coupon is 4.00%, priced at 84.479 to yield 4.900%, maturing in February 2065. This was the seventeenth reopening of a line first issued in September 2024. That series now stands at C$9.0B on its own.

The syndicate is worth reading. RBC led. National Bank and TD were co-leads. BMO, CIBC, Scotia, Desjardins, Laurentian and Casgrain filled out the book. Every major Canadian dealer is underwriting this, which follows when one provincial utility is carrying a 10,000 MW wind target plus the transmission to move the power.

It also shows where private capital does not fit. Hydro-Québec borrows for forty years in the public market at terms no project sponsor can match. Private money enters further down the structure: developer equity, partnership stakes, and the project debt behind tenders like A/O 2026-01, where bids close in February.

title: Transurban spent three years exiting the A25. La Caisse bought both halves.
paragraphs: Transurban, an Australian toll-road operator, sold half of the A25 concession to La Caisse in 2023. In June 2026 it sold the rest for C$280M in equity. Operations moved to Plenary Americas, which La Caisse also owns. A foreign investor is now completely out of one of only two public-private tolled highways in Quebec, and the provincial fund owns all of it and runs it through its own operator.

Boralex followed the same path with more steps visible. La Caisse has been both a shareholder and a lender there since 2017. In July 2025, it and Fondaction put C$250M of subordinated debt into the company. Eight months later it agreed to take Boralex private alongside Brookfield, rolling its stake from roughly 15% to 30%. Lender, then shareholder, then owner.

Put those next to Innergex and the pattern is hard to miss. Outside capital is not being kept out. It is being bought out in stages, on friendly terms, by an institution with a longer horizon and a mandate that is not only financial.
For anyone lending to or investing in Quebec infrastructure, the question is not whether you can get in. It is what your exit looks like, and who will be buying when you want one.

title: Outside capital is not taking over Quebec's mid-market. It is being bought out.
paragraphs: The easy story is that foreign money is pouring into Quebec. The transactions say otherwise, and Innergex is the clearest example. Before the take-private, Hydro-Québec already held about 19.9% and CDPQ was the second largest shareholder, having first invested in 1995. CDPQ then bought the rest at C$13.75 a share, an enterprise value of C$10.0B, and syndicated up to 20% of what it had invested to Investissement Québec, Desjardins Global Asset Management and Fondaction, along with 14 Swiss institutions. Foreign capital was not excluded. It was admitted at a size someone else chose.

Boralex followed the same logic. Brookfield did not buy around La Caisse, it bought with La Caisse, which rolled roughly 15% up to 30% of the private company, and the head office stays in Quebec. The C$1.8B eStruxture recapitalization brought in new capital while the Wener Family Office and the founding CEO reinvested rather than sold.

Where out-of-province buyers did take control, they did it in two places. Take-privates of listed companies, where a public bid cannot be quietly pre-empted. And digital infrastructure, where the domestic bench is thinner and the capital required is more than a provincial balance sheet wants to carry alone. Even those come with conditions. Blue Wolf and Stonepeak paid C$67.00 a share for Logistec in October 2023, and the announcement pairs a contemplated Investissement Québec participation with a commitment to keep the head office and operations in Quebec.

The next test is A/O 2026-01, with bids closing in February. Watch whether the winning consortia are led by domestic sponsors with foreign money behind them, and whether that shapes the financing structures that follow.

An update three months on. The pattern has held in energy and broken in digital infrastructure. Boralex closed and immediately went shopping in the UK. But in October, La Caisse agreed to take 49.9% of Bell's tower company, deliberately stopping short of control, and separately partnered with Macquarie on Maple and with SMBC on an aircraft leasing platform. Those are not ownership-wall deals. They are a provincial fund taking minority positions alongside global managers, which is the opposite of the behaviour this note described. The wall appears to be specific to Quebec-headquartered energy platforms rather than general to Quebec assets.

One caution on all of this. The pattern rests on five transactions, which is enough to notice and not enough to prove. Treat it as a hypothesis with a test attached rather than a finding. A/O 2026-01 closes bids in February and will either support it or break it.
